question.leadin: Give the following about the Adams family.
question.text: John Adams was married to this early feminist, who advised him to "remember the ladies" in one of their numerous correspondences.
question.clue: This figure once called Alexander Hamilton "a man as ambitious as Julius Caesar" and regularly corresponded with Mercy Otis Warren, who congratulated this person on moving to an "elevated position" after this person left Quincy for Philadelphia.

swap.leadin: Answer some questions about famous forts in American history.
swap.text: This fort, located near Lake Champlain in New York, was captured by the Green Mountain Boys led by Ethan Allen in 1775. A popular brand of pencils also shares this name.
swap.clue: This fort's location near Lake Champlain made it useful in monitoring trade routes between New York and Canada.

question.text: Attucks was the first person killed in this event on March 5, 1770. Paul Revere made an engraving showing this event, in which five colonists died in Massachusetts' capital.
question.clue: The engraving The Fruits of Arbitrary Power by Henry Pelham depicts this event by showing a linear arrangement of eight men standing outside a custom house.

swap.leadin: Named for the Chancellor of the Exchequer who proposed them, they were repealed on March 5, 1770, the same day as a notable snowball fight in Massachusetts.
swap.text: Name these Acts of Parliament, designed to pay for British war debts following the Seven Years' War.
swap.clue: The "Massachusetts Circular" letter was written by Samuel Adams in response to this program, and these acts led to the seizure of a sloop owned by John Hancock, the Liberty.

question.text: The Anti-Federalist Papers were partially written by this Virginia politician who staunchly supported states' rights and supposedly declared, "I smell a rat!" during the Constitutional convention.
question.clue: One day after the battles of Lexington and Concord, this man led a local militia against Governor Dunmore to retrieve a batch of stolen gunpowder.

swap.text: This person led a militia that stopped the rebellion. Earlier, this person accepted Charles O'Hara's sword to signify the British surrender at Yorktown.
swap.clue: Though this general commanded the right flank, the Hudson River separated his normal forces from the fighting during the Battle of Saratoga.

question.leadin: The epitaph of the "Boot Monument" commemorates this man's actions but does not name him.
question.text: Name this American general who defected to the British army even after he contributed to a decisive American victory at Saratoga.
question.clue: His most famous action was triggered when he was passed over for a promotion by the Continental Congress and was accused of malfeasance by other officers.

swap.text: Warren sent Revere and Dawes to evacuate John Hancock and this man from Lexington. This man had earlier called a meeting at Faneuil ["FAN-yool"] Hall that sparked an attack on the Dartmouth.
swap.clue: Another of his major projects was extended by Dabney Carr, and was planned with Joseph Warren.

question.leadin: Name these battles featuring George Washington.
question.text: Taking place on August 27, 1776, Washington's forces were decimated by Howe, forcing a retreat to Manhattan.
question.clue: That road was used by Henry Clinton to outflank the American defenders, although he let them escape after declining to attack Brooklyn Heights.

swap.text: This captain of the Bonhomme Richard served as a rear admiral in the Russian Navy before an assault scandal. This man yelled, "I have not yet begun to fight!" when the captain of the Serapis asked him to surrender.
swap.clue: He obtained a reputation for cruelty after flogging the carpenter Mungo Maxwell and running-through the leader of a mutiny, causing him to change his name after fleeing Tobago in 1773.

question.text: This "financier of the revolution" was believed to be one of the conspirators in the Newburgh Conspiracy. He served as Superintendent of Finance during the 1780s, and shares his surname with a founder named "Gouverneur" who wrote the Preamble to the Constitution.
question.clue: The panic of 1797 caused him to fall into debt, though the Bankruptcy Act of 1801 was written specifically to release him from prison.

swap.leadin: This man violated the Proclamation of 1763 when he blazed the Wilderness Road through the Cumberland Gap.
swap.text: Name this American woodsman best known for exploring and organizing the settlement of modern-day Kentucky.
swap.clue: This man partnered with Richard Callaway to track Hanging Maw and the Cherokee who had captured his daughter Jemima.

question.text: Charles O'Hara surrendered the sword of this losing commander at Yorktown. He was the Commander-in-chief during the United Irishmen Rebellion.
question.clue: His namesake "Code" is credited with preventing bureaucratic corruption throughout British rule in India, and he later resigned as viceroy of Ireland in protest over Parliament's denial of Catholic rights.

swap.leadin: Accused of being a loyalist for voting against the Declaration of Independence, he quickly silenced doubters with his "Declaration...Setting Forth the Causes and Necessities of their Taking Up Arms"
swap.text: Name this "Penman of the Revolution" whose wrote a series of letters defending the Constitution under the name Fabius.
swap.clue: Along with Thomas McKean, he was one of the two members of the Continental Congress to enter the military, and he opposed John Adams in the Continental Congress by voting against the Declaration of Independence.

question.leadin: Answer the following about the radio station RTLM.
question.text: Along with the phrase "Crush the cockroaches," RTLM used a code phrase calling for the destruction of "tall" objects of this sort to signal the start of the genocide.
question.clue: A Parson Weems biography relates how a six year old boy destroyed one of these objects.

swap.text: In the Little Egg Harbor Massacre, Ferguson killed 50 sleeping Patriot soldiers under the command of this Polish exile. This Polish nobleman died leading a cavalry charge during the 1779 siege of Savannah.
swap.clue: With Michael Kovats, this Eastern European nobleman reformed the American cavalry during the Revolutionary War.

question.leadin: Answer some questions about the siege of Boston.
question.text: The siege ended soon after Washington ordered fortification of this location with cannons brought from Fort Ticonderoga. Like the Charlestown Heights, this location gave a good view of Boston and its harbor.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about the Committees of Correspondence.
swap.text: Together with Benjamin Franklin and Dr. Arthur Lee, this Connecticut-born man became the first U.S. diplomat sent abroad when he went to France as a secret agent. He had been sent by the so-called Secret Committee, and met with the Comte de Vergennes in 1776 to secure munitions.
swap.clue: This Connecticut Representative who was later fngered by Arthur Lee as a loyalist spy, and may have been assassi-nated by Edward Bancrof.

question.text: This man once pretended to be Banastre Tarleton in order to kill a lot of Loyalist troops during Pyle's Hacking Match. He won a victory at Paulus Hook, New Jersey in 1779 and was later injured defending a Baltimore newspaper from an angry mob
question.answerHtml: Henry Lee III [or Light-Horse Harry Lee or Harry Lee; prompt on just “Lee”]
question.clue: Washington put down the rebellion with the aid of this man, who operated in the southern theater of the Revolutionary War. His nickname came from his competent equestrian skills.

swap.leadin: In this battle, the Comte de Grasse's 24 ship west Indies fleet was reinforced after 3 indecisive days with siege guns fron Newport.
swap.text: Name this battle, named the "decisive battle of the war" by Sir William James, lost by Admiral Thomas Graves.
